extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and grant applicants (faculty, postdocs, research staff) preparing grant revisions and resubmissions
extracted.subtask_description: Practical workshop guidance on interpreting reviewer comments, deciding whether to revise, and how to prepare/resubmit grant proposals to federal agencies (NIH, NSF) and foundations. Covers review criteria, resubmission rules, writing the Introduction, tone/examples, and administrative checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons for proposal rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Your proposal will not be funded. • Your proposal was rejected for administrative reasons. • Your proposal was not a good fit. • You are not equipped with adequate resources. • You failed to convey ‘intellectual merit’. • Your budget does not align with your proposed scope of work. • Presentation, presentation, presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list to diagnose why an application was declined; both substantive (fit, resources, intellectual merit, budget) and administrative/presentation issues can cause rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat rejection as an opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal rejection is complex but useful. AN OPPORTUNITY TO: • Learn from your mistakes • Understand someone else’s perspective (AKA the Reviewers) and see that they are not always wrong • Know the rules of the peer review “system” and use them to your advantage • Cultivate your determination and develop an intentional strategy to be successful
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame rejection constructively to motivate revision strategy rather than as a personal failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess reviews for positivity and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Were the reviews generally positive? Do the strengths outweigh the weaknesses? What types of issues were identified by the reviewers? Why was the proposal rejected? Are there consistencies among the comments?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look across reviews to see whether weaknesses are fixable, whether comments converge on the same problems, and whether strengths can be emphasized in a resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality of reviews (reviewer variability and panel fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: • Reviewers are human too. • Reviewers may disagree with each other. • A poor panel fit could lead to an unhelpful review of a relatively strong proposal. • Negative reviews may not necessarily cover all of the proposal’s weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider panel composition and potential misfits when interpreting critiques; identify which comments are robust versus idiosyncratic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key self-assessment questions after a declination
rubrics_metrics.description: Were the reviewers right? Can you see their point? What did the reviewers generally agree upon? Any outlier comments? Were the reviewers wrong or did your proposal simply not articulate what you had hoped? Did the reviewers misinterpret text or an illustration? Did you fail to include detail that would have addressed reviewer concerns? Can reviewer concerns be rectified? Is the overall tone of the review positive?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these targeted questions to decide whether to resubmit and to prioritize revisions (fixable vs fatal problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative considerations before revising
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Are there a maximum number of submissions/resubmissions allowed? 2. Have I reached the resubmission limit for this particular agency? 3. Is this specific funding mechanism/RFP/program still available? a. If closed, is the program expected to open again? When? b. If not, what are the future deadlines? 4. Is my proposal time-sensitive? a. Does the resubmission window work with my own time constraints?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also remember: funding occurs approximately 6-9 months from date of resubmission for federal sponsors. Check agency-specific limits and timelines before committing to revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatally flawed proposal indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: • The proposed research is neither important nor innovative. • The hypothesis is not supported by pilot data or others’ work. • The literature review was incomplete, outdated, or resulted in conclusions that were not evidence-based. • The proposed research has already been completed by someone else or replicates existing or previously completed research. • The proposed methods are not suitable for testing the stated hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reviews identify any of these as true, resubmission may require substantial new work or reconsideration of the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF resubmission expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: • A declined proposal may be resubmitted after substantial revision • Revised proposals are *NEW* proposals - same standard review procedures • Return to sender: if a resubmitted proposal has not addressed major comments/concerns of prior NSF review or if the moratorium has not ended • Some programs that accept proposals any time may have rules of when declined proposal can be resubmitted • Agency-specific resubmission policies • If a PO confirms – applicant may want to include an Introduction paragraph explaining changes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you substantially address prior reviewer concerns; include an introduction explaining changes when appropriate; be mindful of program-specific rules and moratoria.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF review criteria (panel summary elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical NSF panel summary includes: • Description of the Project • Intellectual Merit • Broader Impact • Summary Statement • Score • Categorization (Not Competitive, Low Competitive, Competitive, Highly Competitive)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand where your proposal fell in categorizations: Not Competitive (probably should not resubmit), Low Competitive (resubmission possible with major overhaul), Competitive (may need attention), Highly Competitive (probably funded; if not, find out why).

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF two core criteria: Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The NSF review process centers on: 1. Intellectual Merit 2. Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address both criteria clearly in resubmissions; reviewers evaluate novelty, significance, rigor (intellectual merit) and societal/educational impacts (broader impacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH review core criteria and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance – Investigator(s) – Innovation – Approach – Environment. Overall Impact or Criterion Strength scored 1–9 with descriptors (1 Exceptional … 9 Poor). Impact Score guidance: Impact Score (average of all reviewer impact scores x10) — 10–30: likely to be funded; 31–45: occasionally funded; 46+: almost never funded. Percentile indicates % of proposals with a better impact score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the five core criteria to structure revisions. Aim to reduce key weaknesses that drive overall impact; consult the Impact Score guide (including factors such as enthusiasm, fixability, timing, panel fit) to estimate resubmission prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH resubmission policy rules
rubrics_metrics.description: • Only one resubmission (A1) of an original application (A0) will be accepted. • A1 applications can be submitted to any program announcement that accepts resubmissions so long as eligibility and other requirements are met. • Review criteria will be used from the current FOA (vs the criteria of the A0 FOA). • Subsequent resubmission should reflect how the field has changed; include new preliminary data, relevant literature, letters of reference. • The activity code may not change between A0 and A1 (unless FOA changes). • Resubmissions must be submitted within 37 months of the original A0; an A1 must not be submitted until the Summary Statement of the A0 has been received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these formal constraints carefully; failure to comply can make a resubmission ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction to the resubmission (format and content)
rubrics_metrics.description: A resubmission should include a 1-page Introduction: • A summary of substantial additions, deletions, and changes to the application • A response to weaknesses raised in the Summary Statement. • A different application title is allowable. • A PD/PI can be added or removed. • Identifying individual changes in the text is not needed. • Use most current forms. • Provide substantive justification as to why you disagree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be brief and direct; highlight the most important concerns; use reviewer numbers (R1, R2, R3); refer to proposal sections; use active voice and plural first-person (“we”); ask your Program Officer if unsure and have a colleague read the response. Note exceptions: some K/R25/T/D applications allow a 3-page intro.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to write the sample Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Include title and proposal number of original submission; thank reviewers; emphasize strengths and positive comments; address critique — all of it; use Reviewer numbers; most important concerns should receive the most space; make sure responses refer to a section of your proposal; be brief and direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a short sample phrasing as model; highlight changes in the proposal and quote positive reviewer lines if helpful; do not over-apologize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make substantive changes in the body, not just the Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t forget to make changes in the body of the proposal! Check and double-check this because the reviewers will. ….unless the Reviewers told you to delete something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers will check that changes discussed in the Intro are present in the main application; update text, figures, and budgets accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and framing: respond, don’t defend
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondive example vs Defensive example shown: e.g., when asked for a 6-month follow-up, a defensive reply rejects the idea; a responsive reply acknowledges the point, adds a feasible compromise, and explains constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing reviewer criticisms, acknowledge the concern, explain changes or constraints politely, and offer concrete adjustments rather than defensive rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting reviewer misinterpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers missed information, avoid defensive phrasing like “We already included X” and instead clarify lack of clarity and indicate where the information will be presented (e.g., 'We will include age as a matching criteria. Specifically... (see Section C.4 Study Design)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the resubmission to clarify wording and point reviewers to the exact sections so misinterpretations are resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to address criticism by proposal section
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers were critical of: • Significance: Emphasize how project addresses a key gap in knowledge and aligns with funder’s mission. • Methods: Update preliminary findings, present methods to match aims/objectives, explain design decisions, identify challenges and alternatives. • Experience: Discuss relevant experience, upload biosketches, recruit collaborators or consultants, consider interdisciplinary approach, integrate an Advisory Board. • Presentation: Beef up the Project Description with GREAT graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor revisions to the specific criterion flagged by reviewers; add data, personnel, or clarity as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative 'Don’t forgets' checklist before resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: • Solicit new Letters of Support • Use any new templates and follow any new guidelines/requirements • Update Biographical Sketches • Do not obsess over prior critiques • Ask for outside help and peer reviewers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all documents are current and that supporting materials reflect changes; get external reviews to spot lingering weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation-specific approach and cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: • A foundation generally does not provide reviewer comments and the reason for rejection may not be provided. • They often lack clear definition for their criteria and processes. • A foundation may or may not have a program officer. • As a general rule, foundations typically prefer pre-application contact. • Revisit your proposal after the rejection. • Ask a trusted colleague to review the proposal and provide feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For foundations, cultivate relationships before, during, and after the formal grant process; plan timelines and consider adding new collaborators; expect less formal feedback and rely on networking and pre-submission contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative pathways after rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: • Identify a different study section within the same agency • Submit to another opportunity within the same funding agency • Submit to another funder – A poor program fit could lead to a poor review of a good proposal • Move on from that project (don’t throw good effort after bad) • Design a pilot project to help demonstrate feasibility (work with your Center for Research Design and Analysis (CRDA))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resubmission is not feasible or likely to succeed, consider re-targeting, piloting, or abandoning the project strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key points for overall strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: • Expect it — Grants rarely get funded on initial submission • Accept it — Reviewer is ALWAYS right, even when he or she isn’t; Reviewers will always find flaws • Perfect it — Develop a plan; Successfully address concerns
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a mindset and workflow: expect rejection, use feedback productively, and plan resubmission activities early (start planning the minute you submit).
